source.title: Dynamic Guided and Domain Applicable Safeguards for Enhanced Security in Large Language Models
source.authors: Weidi Luo; He Cao; Zi-Jing Liu; Yu Wang; Ai-Dan Wong; Bing Feng; Yuan Yao; Yu Li

record.file_problem: No apparent cutoff or wrong-document issue. Some tables are flattened in the provided text, but their row and column values can be assigned from the layout and the accompanying discussion.
record.tranche_reason: Reports harmful-response rates for GCG jailbreak attacks, an adversarial-suffix attack, on models with and without inference-stage defenses. This conceptually tests whether that kind of attack can bypass safety, but it does not measure the proposed first-token mechanism.
record.gate_note: Rows below cover GCG only, because it is the listed general attack that directly uses an optimized adversarial suffix. Results for other attacks are not evidence about the specific compliant-opening, suffix, or decoding bypass described in V4. The paper does not measure token-position KL, compliant prefilling, or decoding changes.
record.test_reason: This is a defense paper. It uses existing jailbreak attack sets, including precomputed GCG suffixes, as a test bed for its own inference-stage defense (G4D) and reports that defense's ASR against baselines. The main general-attack subset was selected to include only attacks already successful on GPT-4o-mini, GPT-3.5 and LLaMA-3-8B. So the no-defense ASRs are partly built in by selection rather than measured as a fresh bypass rate. The paper does not ask whether getting past the opening defeats refusal. It runs no prefilling, decoding or token-position analysis, and no fine-tuning.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that G4D, a three-agent inference-stage defense (intention detector, paraphraser, retrieval-grounded safety analyzer), lowers jailbreak ASR in general and chemistry/biology settings while keeping benign-task performance. They add that it complements output-stage defenses such as AutoDefense.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates inference-stage prompting and defense agents against jailbreak attacks; it does not use fine-tuning, token-position KL measurement, or first-token prefilling.
record.method_sensitivity: GCG ASR varies with the victim model, defense method, and general-attack dataset (main subset versus total set).
record.peer_reviewed: North American Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics
record.problems: The main general-attack results use a selected subset containing only attacks successful on GPT-3.5, GPT-4o-mini, and LLaMA-3-8B; the GCG subset has n=6. The paper reports no uncertainty estimates. GCG ASR is an attack outcome, not a test of why safety may be bypassed, and no compliant-prefix or decoding-change experiment is reported.
record.rows_left_out: Other attack types and non-GCG aggregates are omitted because they do not specifically test the adversarial-suffix component of V4. Benign-task outcomes and domain-specific ASR are omitted because they do not measure the behavior named by V4.

untested.parts: No per-token KL or position analysis.
No prefilling, decoding manipulation, or analysis of whether suffix success works by passing the opening tokens. GCG prompts are reused from earlier datasets and preselected for success.
No analysis of the causes of shallowness.
No deepening training. G4D is a prompt-level, inference-stage defense.

record.verdict_notes: I checked the GCG column assignments in the flattened Table 2 against the text, which cites G4D Vicuna GCG 16.7, CB-RedTeam 53.3→1.3 and AutoDAN 2.5. The record's GCG values (GPT-4o-mini 83.0, Vicuna 100) and the Table 9 total-set values are correct. The reader's V4 'supports' label rests on preselected subsets and baseline references, and its 'limits_scope' label rests on defense comparisons. Neither bears on V4, so I give no verdict.

versions.untested_parts: Harmful fine-tuning and safety refusal after fine-tuning.
Benign fine-tuning and its effect on harmful compliance.
Per-token KL divergence between aligned and base models on harmful prompts.

The study reports GCG adversarial-suffix attack outcomes, but does not test compliant prefilling or decoding changes, nor whether success is specifically caused by passing the opening response tokens.
Whether safety is localized in a small set of weights or ranks.
Whether data or training objectives produce safety shallowness.
Training intended to deepen safety and its robustness.

relation.reason: Existing jailbreak vulnerability supplies the defense test bed; the paper reports safeguard performance without testing the proposed concentration or training mechanisms.

tranche.reason: The study reuses jailbreak attacks to evaluate inference-stage safeguards. Its experiments compare defense performance rather than independently examine a shallow-alignment claim.

source_check.notes: The reported ASRs match the checked cells, but defense comparisons should not be counted as independent phenomenon results. Selection limits the main subset's interpretation; absence of an opening-token analysis alone would not exclude V4, whose wording also includes suffix attacks.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: GCG attack with no defense, GPT-4o-mini and Vicuna-v1.5-13B, subset and total-set evaluations
reader_labels.reason: GCG produced harmful-response ASRs of 83.0 and 100 on the subset, and 67.3 on the total set, showing bypasses in these tested settings (r1, r7, r13).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: GCG attack under the reported defenses
reader_labels.reason: Success was not uniform: some defenses reduced GCG ASR to 0.0, while other results varied by model and dataset (r2-r6, r8-r12, r14-r21). The paper does not establish a first-token cause or test prefilled openings or decoding changes.
